prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect

statement.case_for: Topological insulators are a discovery in the sense the prize asks for: a new class of electronic matter with a clear theoretical origin (the Kane-Mele Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall proposal) and a decisive laboratory realization (Molenkamp's HgTe edge channels). Five of the six colleagues who ranked it placed it first or third, and four proposed the Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio, so the opening ballots already converge on a fairly compact attribution. Two decades of independent confirmation by transport, ARPES and scanning probe methods, and the way the concept has spread through materials science, make this mature rather than premature. From my own bench, the direct imaging of edge and surface states is exactly the type of experimental fingerprint that turns a theory into a physical discovery.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Three slots cannot hold Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that guided the HgTe experiment is outside the credited names, as are Fu, Moore and Balents for the three-dimensional case. Whichever trio we choose, the prize will look incomplete to part of the community, and the committee must be comfortable that a Kane, Mele, Molenkamp citation is defensible when the original sources of the HgTe prediction are not credited. There is also a framing overlap with the quantum anomalous Hall entry, which risks splitting support.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B041 first and favours Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, accepting that this leaves Mele out in order to credit the first three-dimensional topological insulator experiments.
responses.response: I made the same choice in my opening ballot, but I have reconsidered it. The Kane-Mele paper is a joint original contribution to the Z2 idea and the quantum spin Hall proposal, and omitting Mele is hard to defend on the principle that the prize identifies the people responsible for the original work. Hasan's ARPES work is a genuine and important experimental discovery, but the three-dimensional case rests on a theory chain (Fu, Kane, Mele and Moore, Balents) that is not wholly inside our credited set, so crediting Hasan without that chain is less clean than crediting the theory pair plus the first experimental realization. I therefore move from Hasan to Mele, while recognizing that this is the point on which I and Danielsson still differ.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B041 first as a new organising principle for electronic matter, proposes Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and notes that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal sits outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree with the trio and with the caveat on Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and I would add that the committee should say openly in its citation wording that the prize covers the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators broadly, not a single paper. I would qualify his remark that recognition is overdue: it is mature, but that does not by itself answer why this should come before the second-ranked candidates, such as the dynamical mean-field or moire entries he and others favour. For those, the case is still contested on mechanism, which is the difference I rely on.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B029 first, a configuration of Kane, Molenkamp and Xue that combines the quantum spin Hall and quantum anomalous Hall effects, and omits Mele.
responses.response: I share his instinct that the topological band concept is the key idea, but I disagree with folding the quantum anomalous Hall effect into the same prize. Xue's observation is a notable second-generation result that depends on magnetic doping and ultra-low temperatures, and it follows the discoveries it extends. B041 gives a tighter story: prediction, first experimental observation, then confirmation in many materials. Adding a QAH name to the citation would also force out Mele, whose credit I consider more fundamental than the later extension.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first and B041 third, noting that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe state that Molenkamp observed, and that Hasan demonstrated the 3D phases.
responses.response: Her note on Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is the fairest statement of the attribution problem, and I do not think it can be fully resolved within the supplied names. On her first choice, the lattice clock, I agree that Katori's magic-wavelength proposal is a clean invention and I ranked it second, so it is my first alternative. Where I differ is that I treat the redefinition of the second as an argument for waiting for that outcome rather than as evidence for priority now, since the practical case is still partly in the future while the topological case is already settled.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can accept omitting Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (HgTe prediction) and Hasan (3D materials) from a Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio.
Whether the quantum anomalous Hall entry should be treated as part of the same achievement or as a later separate development.
I rely on memory for the detailed priority chronology and have not independently verified individual claims.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for the preferred configuration. My general connections are Chalmers colleagues (including fellow committee member Johansson), David Clarke at IBM, Japanese academic exchanges and the international microscopy federation, and none of these involves the credited names for B041, B013 or B014 as far as the profile shows.
